title: We hymn only God and His Word
source_text: Ἵνα δὲ καὶ τροπολογῆται καὶ λέγηται φρόνησις εἶναι ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ, παραστησάτω τις αὐτῆς τὴν ὑπόστασιν καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν, ὡς ὑφεστηκυίας κατὰ τὴν τροπολογίαν ταύτην. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀρχαία τις γενομένη ἄνθρωπος ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ τετίμηται, παραδόντων τοῖς ὑποχειρίοις μυστήρια καὶ τελετὰς τῶν βουληθέντων αὐτῆς τὸ ὄνομα παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ὡς θεοῦ ᾄδεσθαι, πολλῷ μᾶλλον οὐ χρὴ ὑμνῆσαι καὶ ὡς θεὸν δοξάσαι τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν, εἴ γε οὐδὲ τὸν τηλικοῦτον ἥλιον προσκυνεῖν ἡμῖν θέμις, κἂν εὐφημῶμεν αὐτόν. Κέλσος μὲν οὖν φησι μᾶλλον ἡμᾶς σέβειν δοκεῖν τὸν μέγαν θεὸν, ἂν καὶ Ἥλιον καὶ Ἀθηνᾶν ὑμνῶμεν, ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸ ἐναντίον ἴσμεν. ὕμνους γὰρ εἰς μόνον τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι λέγομεν θεὸν καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ αὐτοῦ θεὸν λόγον. καὶ ὑμνοῦμέν γε θεὸν καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ αὐτοῦ ὡς καὶ „ἥλιος καὶ σελήνη“ καὶ „ἄστρα“ καὶ πᾶσα ἡ οὐρανία στρατιά. ὑμνοῦσι γὰρ πάντες οὗτοι, θεῖος ὄντες χορὸς, μετὰ τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις δικαίων τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ αὐτοῦ. προείπομεν μὲν οὖν μὴ δεῖν ὀμνύναι τὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις βασιλέα ἢ τὴν ὀνομαζομένην τύχην αὐτοῦ. διὸ οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον ἡμᾶς πάλιν ἀπολογεῖσθαι πρὸς τὸ κἂν ἐν ἀνθρώποις βασιλέα κελεύῃ σέ τις ὁρκωμοτεῖν, οὐδὲ τοῦτο δεινόν. δέδοται γὰρ τούτῳ τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς, καὶ ὅ τι ἂν λαμβάνῃς ἐν τῷ βίῳ, παρὰ τούτου λαμβάνεις. ἡμεῖς δέ φαμεν ὅτι οὐ πάντως δέδοται τούτῳ τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς ὅλα, οὐδ᾿ ὅ τι ἂν λαμβάνωμεν ἐν τῷ βίῳ, παρὰ τούτου λαμβάνομεν. δικαίως γὰρ καὶ καλῶς λαμβάνοντες, ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῆς προνοίας αὐτοῦ λαμβάνομεν, οἷον ἡμέρους καρποὺς καὶ ἄρτον, στηρίζοντα „καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου,“ καὶ τὴν προσηνῆ ἄμπελον καὶ οἶνον, εὐφραίνοντα „καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς τῆς ἐλαίας καρποὺς ἀπὸ τῆς προνοίας ἔχομεν τοῦ θεοῦ „τοῦ ἱλαρῦναι πρόσωπον ἐν ἐλαίῳ.“
pass_a_gloss: And even if it is allegorised (τροπολογέω) and Athena is said to be prudence/wisdom (φρόνησις), let someone present (παρίστημι) her subsistence (ὑπόστασις) and essence (οὐσία), as of one subsisting (ὑφίσταμαι) according to this allegory (τροπολογία). But if Athena, having been some ancient human being, has been honoured (τιμάω), those wishing her name to be sung (ᾄδω) among men as of a god having handed down (παραδίδωμι) to their subjects (ὑποχείριοι) mysteries (μυστήρια) and initiations (τελεταί), much more one ought not to hymn and glorify (δοξάζω) Athena as a god, if indeed it is not lawful (θέμις) for us even to worship/do obeisance to (προσκυνέω) the so great sun, even if we praise (εὐφημέω) it. Celsus then says that we seem more to revere the great God if we hymn both Helios and Athena, but we know the opposite. For hymns we speak to only the God over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) and his only-begotten (μονογενής) God Word (θεὸς λόγος). And we hymn God and his Only-begotten as also 'sun and moon' and 'stars' and all the heavenly host (οὐρανία στρατιά). For all these hymn, being a divine choir (χορός), with the righteous (δίκαιοι) among men, the God over all and his Only-begotten. We said before, then, that one must not swear by the king among men or his so-called fortune. Therefore it is not necessary for us again to defend ourselves (ἀπολογέομαι) against: 'And even if someone commands you to swear an oath (ὁρκωμοτέω) by a king among men, not even this is terrible (δεινός). For to him have been given the things on earth, and whatever you receive in life, you receive from him.' But we say that not at all (οὐ πάντως) have all the things on earth been given to him, nor whatever we receive in life do we receive from him. For receiving justly and rightly (καλῶς), we receive from God and his providence (πρόνοια), such as cultivated (ἥμερος) fruits and bread, strengthening (στηρίζω) 'the heart of man', and the gentle (προσηνής) vine and wine, gladdening (εὐφραίνω) 'the heart of man'. But also the fruits of the olive we have from the providence of God, 'to make cheerful (ἱλαρύνω) the face with oil'.
pass_b_english: Even if Athena is allegorised and said to be wisdom, let someone establish her real existence and her substance, showing that she subsists in the way this allegory says. And if Athena was once a woman of ancient times and has been honoured because those who wished her name to be sung among men as a goddess handed down mysteries and rites to their subjects, then all the more ought we not to hymn Athena and glorify her as a goddess, since it is not lawful for us even to worship the sun, great as it is, though we praise it.

Celsus, then, says that we seem the more to worship the great God if we hymn both the Sun and Athena; but we know the opposite. For we sing hymns only to the God over all and to His only-begotten, God the Word (compare John 1:1; John 1:18). And we hymn God and His Only-begotten, as do also “sun and moon” and “stars” (Psalm 148:3) and the whole heavenly host (compare Luke 2:13). For all these, being a divine choir, together with the righteous among men, hymn the God over all and His Only-begotten.

We said before that we must not swear by the king among men, or by what is called his fortune. So we need not defend ourselves again against this: “And even if someone commands you to take an oath by a king among men, not even this is anything terrible. For to him have been given the things on earth, and whatever you receive in this life, you receive from him.” But we say that it is by no means true that all things on earth have been given to him, nor do we receive from him whatever we receive in this life. For whatever we receive justly and rightly, we receive from God and His providence: cultivated crops, and bread that “strengthens the heart of man,” and the gentle vine, and wine that “gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 104:15). The fruit of the olive too we have from the providence of God, “to make the face shine with oil” (Psalm 104:15).

choices.choice: ‘His only-begotten, God the Word’ renders τὸν μονογενῆ αὐτοῦ θεὸν λόγον; the phrase echoes John 1:18 (μονογενὴς θεός, in the reading Origen knew) and John 1:1; cited with ‘compare’ as allusions. ‘Sun and moon’ and ‘stars’ are drawn from Psalm 148:3 (same number in LXX and English); ‘the whole heavenly host’ echoes Luke 2:13 (στρατιᾶς οὐρανίου, a host praising God), compare also Psalm 148:2. Psalm 104:15 = LXX Psalm 103:15 (bread strengthens the heart, wine gladdens the heart, oil makes the face cheerful); the citation is given after the bread-and-wine clause and again after the oil clause, since all three phrases come from the one verse. ‘a woman of ancient times’ renders ἀρχαία τις γενομένη ἄνθρωπος (ἄνθρωπος with feminine article: a human being, here a woman). ‘as a goddess’ renders ὡς θεοῦ and ὡς θεόν (θεός serves for both genders). The Celsus quotation about the king is his own continuous argument (compare 8.63, 8.65); the Greek introduces it only as ‘against this’ (πρὸς τό), without naming him. οὐ πάντως rendered ‘by no means’; an alternative reading is ‘not in every respect’. φρόνησις rendered ‘wisdom’ (the Stoic allegory of Athena as practical wisdom).
'Even if the story is allegorised' -> 'Even if Athena is allegorised' (subject is Athena)
'as of one who subsists according to this allegory' -> 'showing that she subsists in the way this allegory says' (calque removed)
'glorify her as a god' -> 'as a goddess' (consistent with the preceding ὡς θεοῦ)
'to the God over all alone, and to His only-begotten Word, who is God' -> 'only to the God over all and to His only-begotten, God the Word' (μόνον governs both; old order read as a contradiction)
Psalm 104:15 citation added beside the bread-and-wine clause as well as the oil clause
Psalm 148:3, LXX 103:15 -> English 104:15, Luke 2:13 checked: correct

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
